title: Relative Risk: "Doubles Your Risk!"
objective: After this level you can explain why "doubles your risk" can mean going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000, and ask for the absolute numbers.
summary: Relative risk compares groups ("doubles", "triples") but hides how likely the thing is. From a tiny start, even tripling adds few cases, so always ask for the absolute risks.

cards.headline: "Doubles your risk!" Doubles it from what?
cards.body: Going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 is doubling. So is going from 1 in 10 to 2 in 10. Same headline, wildly different news. This level shows you how to tell them apart.

cards.headline: Relative risk: a comparison, not a chance
cards.body: Relative risk compares two groups: the risk in one against the risk in the other. A relative risk of 1 means no difference; 2 means twice as likely. That is useful for spotting what matters. But it tells you how many times, not how many people. On its own, a relative risk says nothing about how likely the thing is at all.

cards.headline: "Triple the risk" in a real headline
cards.body: In 2012, a study of more than 175,000 young people found that repeated CT scans in childhood could triple the risk of leukemia and brain tumors. Scary. Now the absolute numbers: about one extra case of each for every 10,000 head scans in children aged 10 or under, over the next 10 years. The researchers stressed that when a child needs a scan, its benefits should outweigh that small risk.

cards.fact: Tiny start, big multiplier, small change.
cards.context: When a risk starts very small, even tripling it adds few cases. When it starts big, a modest rise can hit many people: doubling 1 in 10 means 1,000 extra cases per 10,000 people. So when you hear "doubles" or "triples", ask for the two absolute risks, before and after.

cards.headline: Relative risk: decoded
learned: "Doubles" says how many times, not how many people
CT study: triple the risk, about 1 extra case per 10,000 scans
Ask for both absolute risks, before and after

questions.prompt: What does a relative risk compare?

options.label: The risk in one group with the risk in another
The number of cases with the size of the population
options.rationale: Dividing cases by the population gives a rate or an absolute risk.

options.label: A risk today with the highest risk ever recorded
options.rationale: It compares two groups, not a record.

options.label: How often a risk is reported with how often it happens
options.rationale: Reporting has nothing to do with it.

questions.explanation: Relative risk puts two groups side by side: 2 means one group is twice as likely as the other.

questions.prompt: Why can "triples the risk" still mean only a few extra cases?

options.label: Tripling only counts in very large studies
options.rationale: Study size doesn't change what tripling means.

options.label: Relative risks are always rounded down
options.rationale: No rounding is involved; the starting risk is what matters.

options.label: Studies overstate every risk by three times
options.rationale: The tripling was a real finding; it just started from a tiny risk.

options.label: The starting risk was very small

questions.explanation: Tripling a tiny risk still leaves a small one: about one extra case per 10,000 scans in the CT study.

questions.prompt: Level 5 showed that a risk going from 10% to 15% rose by 5 percentage points. As a relative change, that rise is _____.

options.label: 5% higher
options.rationale: That mixes up points and percent; 5 ÷ 10 is 0.5.

options.label: 15% higher
options.rationale: The new risk is 15%, but the rise compared with the start is bigger.

options.label: 150% higher
options.rationale: 15% is one and a half times 10%, which is a 50% rise.

questions.explanation: Absolute change: 5 points. Relative change: 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5, a 50% rise. Same event, two very different-sounding numbers.
